extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, science journalists, and members of the public interested in post-publication peer review and research integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and observed norms for commenting on and using PubPeer as a platform for post-publication peer review of scientific research. Covers site policies (e.g., anonymity, fact-verification), typical content types (misconduct, methodological critique), and downstream responses by authors and journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review (genre)
rubrics_metrics.description: PubPeer is a website that allows users to discuss and review scientific research after publication, i.e. post-publication peer review, established in 2012.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames the work: comments and discussions are meant to critique published scientific research. Use the platform for critique and discussion of published results rather than as a venue for pre-publication review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use only facts that can be publicly verified
rubrics_metrics.description: The website has since 2016 told commentators to use only facts that can be publicly verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit site policy to reduce legal exposure and discourage unsubstantiated accusations — commenters should cite verifiable evidence (figures, data, text) rather than hearsay or private allegations. This functions as both an ethical and legal guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymous commenting allowed (policy and consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to most platforms, it allows anonymous post-publication commenting, a controversial feature which is the main factor for its success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymity enables whistleblowing and may increase reporting of issues but also raises concerns (libel accusations, transparency). Users should weigh benefits and risks; platform permits anonymity while warning about verifiable facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of legal risk (libel accusations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accusations of libel have been levelled at some of PubPeer's users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because comments can allege misconduct, commenters and the platform face legal risks. This is the reason behind the 2016 guidance to use only publicly verifiable facts. Avoid defamatory language and unsupported allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common acceptable/observed content types: reports of misconduct and image manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2021 study found that 'more than two-thirds of comments [on PubPeer] are posted to report some type of misconduct, mainly about image manipulation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On-topic, high-impact comments often document concrete problems such as image manipulation; providing clear, evidentiary examples (annotated figures, comparisons) aligns with platform norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline-specific uses: methodological critique and theory discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Social science and humanities disciplines had fewer comments, but the highest percentage comments about critical reviews about theory and highlight methodological flaws. The research concluded that 'social scientists and humanists use it to discuss conclusions and detect methodological errors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable content in these fields tends to be conceptual/theoretical critique and identification of methodological weaknesses rather than allegations of data manipulation. Tailor critiques to disciplinary norms (theory, methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect limited author engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The study reported that 85.6% of comments are anonymous and that 'only 31.5% of publications received more than three comments, and the response rate of authors is very low (7.5%).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume authors will respond; design comments to be clear and self-contained so they remain useful even without author reply. If seeking correction or clarification, consider also contacting authors or journals via formal channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited downstream editorial correction rate
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2023 a study found that 'only 21.5% of the articles [flagged on PubPeer] that deserve an editorial notice (i.e., honest errors, methodological flaws, publishing fraud, manipulation) were corrected by the [relevant] journal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users should be aware that raising issues on PubPeer does not guarantee journal action; when correction or retraction is sought, parallel contact with editors or formal complaints may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright and ownership concerns for (often-anonymous) content
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions have been raised about the copyright ownership of PubPeer's often-anonymous contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters and researchers reposting PubPeer material should consider copyright/ownership implications; anonymous contributions complicate attribution and rights. Platform users and third parties should check terms of service and applicable copyright law before reuse.
